text: AWS Capstone's own disaster-recovery lesson names an honest RPO and RTO for a nightly batch pipeline. Driftwood's platform needs the same honesty -- but Snowflake gives you a genuinely different, built-in recovery mechanism to reason about instead of restoring from a separate backup.

Driftwood's raw, staging, and marts tables are all permanent, not transient -- a deliberate choice. Unlike a reload-from-source staging table, Driftwood's raw tables are the only copy of a given day's billing export once the source file is gone. That single fact justifies paying for permanent tables' full fail-safe and time-travel window everywhere in this project.

This is Driftwood's single most likely real incident: a dbt model ran with a bug and overwrote marts.dim_subscribers with wrong data. Time Travel's AT OFFSET syntax queries the table as it existed two hours ago, directly -- no separate backup system, no restore request, just a SQL query. Confirmed good, clone it back.

UNDROP reverses an accidental DROP TABLE completely -- but only inside the time-travel window. With a one-day retention, that's a same-day recovery only. Past that window, fail-safe's seven additional days still hold the data, but recovering from it means contacting Snowflake support directly -- genuine disaster recovery, not a convenient undo button.
That's exactly why the self-service time-travel window is the setting actually worth tuning, rather than relying on fail-safe as if it were routine.

Neither mechanism protects against a mistake in the source data itself. If Driftwood's billing platform sends a corrupted export and the pipeline's own validation doesn't catch it, time travel can restore the table to exactly how it looked yesterday -- built from that same corrupted export. That's why load validation and dbt tests exist as a separate layer of defense.
Next lesson: presenting this entire platform in an interview -- the five-beat story that ties all thirteen lessons together.
